steps: Uncrate
Remove the crate top, supports and plastic cover, then the lag bolts holding the unit to the pallet (7/16"(12mm) wrench).
Fit the side panels
Pattern at the top: guide the front tabs into the slots on the panel mounting brackets, pull back to engage, then screw at the rear. Use the fibre washers on enamel panels to prevent chipping.
Floor protection

Continuous non-combustible ember protection on a combustible floor: USA 16" front and 8" to the sides of the door opening; Canada 18" firing side, 8" other sides; under the connector plus 2" each side.
Position to clearances
Set the floor protector and stove to the clearance diagram. Shielding approved under CSA B365 / NFPA 211 can reduce clearances; for close clearances use a listed double-wall connector.
Mark the flue path
Hang a plumb-bob over the exact centre of the flue to mark the ceiling and roof holes; check joists and rafters, adjust, and reconfirm clearances.
Install the chimney

Listed chimney to its maker's directions, ceiling to rain cap (UL-103 HT in the USA, ULC-S629 in Canada), or a lined masonry chimney. 15 feet minimum system height; exit 3 feet above the roof and two feet above anything within 10 feet.

Listed chimney: ULC-S629 or UL-103HT listed stainless, installed to its maker's directions from the ceiling through to the rain cap (this may include framing in holes). Masonry: lined, suitable for solid fuel, in good condition and to code; have it cleaned and inspected by a professional for cracks, weak mortar or deterioration (Figure 12 shows a 6" S.S. liner).

Flue size6 inches (same as the stove outlet)
Min. system height15 feet (4.6 m.) from base of appliance
Above roof3 feet (1 m.)
Above highest projectiontwo feet (0.6 m.) within 10 feet (3 m.) horizontally

One appliance per flue. Offsets: every joint of listed connector, offset elbows and chimney screwed with at least three sheet metal screws, supported by the chimney maker's listed offset support (Figure 11).
Connect the flue pipe

Slip the crimped edge inside the stove collar and fix with three screws through the collar holes; build up with crimped ends down, 3 sheet metal screws per joint, and the approved adapter at the chimney.

• Single-wall: six inch diameter, 24 gauge black pipe, clean and in new condition, as short and straight as possible.
  • Crimped or male ends pointing down, so liquid creosote or condensation runs back into the stove; 3 sheet metal screws at every joint and collar.
  • Never through an attic, roof space, closet or similar concealed space, floor or ceiling.
  • First section of pipe 12" [300mm] minimum; give it as much vertical length as possible, as the unit may be harder to start (Figure 11).

Through a combustible wall (NFPA 211, pp. 21–22)

System A · brick with fireclay liner12 in. (305mm) to combustibles
System B · insulated listed chimney length9 in. (229mm)
System C · ventilated sheet steel thimble6 in. (152mm)
System D · insulated pass-through, 2 in. larger i.d.2 in. (51mm)

Maintain the vapour barrier wherever components penetrate to the exterior. A wall pass-through must conform to CAN/CSA-B365 or NFPA 211.
Combustion air

Room air through the Ash Box Enclosure, or 4" outside air through the floor or rear wall via the Intake Starter. Required in mobile homes; residential outside air means securing the stove to the structure.
Mobile home extras
Lag the legs or pedestal to the floor (two 1/4" x 2" or longer screws); listed double-wall connector only, no horizontal connector, never in a sleeping room.
Firebrick
Lay the firebrick from the rear wall, then the side walls, then the floor (Figure 18). A gap remains behind the ash dump; one full brick is a spare.

Brick sizes (Figure 18):

A8 7/8" x 4 3/8" x 1 1/4"
B8 7/8" x 2 1/8" x 1 1/4"
C5 3/4" x 4 3/8" x 1 1/4"
D4 3/8" x 3 1/4" x 1 1/4"
E7" x 3 1/4" x 1 1/4"
F4 1/4" x 2 1/8" x 1 1/4"
  1. Rear wall: stand an "A" behind the brick-rail tab and slide it toward the centre; slide a second "A" under the tab; repeat for the rest of the rear wall.
  2. Side walls: an "A" against the side wall up to the rear-wall brick, another "A" beside it, then a narrow "B"; a "D" on top of the "A" bricks, tucked behind the brick rail; an "E" under the rail tab, resting on the three side-wall bricks. Repeat on the other side.
  3. Floor: two "A" bricks, a third "A" against the rear wall, the "C" beside the ash dump against the left-hand wall, then the front row: "F" at the right, "B" in the centre, "F" at the left.

A gap remains behind the ash dump, and one full-size brick is left over as a spare. Firebrick set: part 80002355.

panels.title: Excessive creosote build-up
items: Wood too wet → use dry wood
Air control turned down too soon → wait for a good bed of coals and charred wood
Draft too low → check for a plugged or restricted flue, improper chimney height and/or diameter; provide outside air; check the draft and alter as needed

panels.title: Low heat output
items: Wood may be wet → check it and use drier wood
Fire too small → build a larger fire; open the draft control to increase burn rate
Draft too low → chimney plugged or restricted; inspect and clean

panels.title: Won't burn overnight
items: Air control set too high → set it lower
Not enough wood → unsplit wood is preferred for overnight burns
Draft too high → excessive chimney height and/or diameter (Figures 11, 12)

panels.title: Stove won't burn
items: Combustion air supply blocked → check the outside air supply for obstructions and that the room air cover is removed
Chimney plugged or restricted → inspect and clean

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Never use chemicals or any other volatile liquid to start a fire: no gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene or charcoal lighter fluid.

  1. Move the air control to High (all the way to the left) and open the door.
  2. Put crumpled newspaper in the centre of the stove. Crisscross several pieces of dry kindling on it, then add a few small pieces of dry wood on top.
  3. Light the paper. Leave the door ajar about 1/2" (13mm) to 1" (25mm) until the kindling is fully engulfed in flame.
  4. Add a few small logs and close the door.
  5. Once there's a good bed of coals and the wood has charred, begin normal operation.

Build the fire right on the firebricks, never on a grate or andirons. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine.

Your first 2–3 fires bake on the paint. The smoke and fumes can bother some people, so open all windows and doors and follow the Stove Bright sheet that came with the stove. Smoke detectors may go off more often while the paint cures. Don't disconnect them.

burn.title: Air control, reloading & overnight burns
burn.html:
The air control sets how hard the fire burns, from L (low) to H (high). Every home is different, so your best setting comes from trial and error. Note what works.

  • After each load, leave the air fairly wide open for the first 10 to 30 minutes. After that you can turn it down a lot without much smoke.
  • Smoke pouring down across the glass (a "waterfall") means you turned it down too soon or too low.
  • Use H only to start the fire or preheat a fresh load.

Reloading

Set the air to high and let the fire brighten, then open the door slowly to prevent back puffing. Load logs endwise, up to 18" (457mm), so air can flow between them. Small loads of two or three logs burn cleanest.

Overnight

Use unsplit logs and char them completely on the maximum setting before turning the air down. Never try it with green or wet wood. To restart, rake the embers to the front, add a couple of dry split logs, close the door and set the air to high.

Don't over-fire. A glowing red top or vent pipe means the stove is over-firing. It can permanently damage the stove and chimney and may void the warranty. Keep the door closed whenever it's burning.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only. Air-dried, seasoned hardwood gives higher efficiency and lower emissions than softwood or green, freshly cut hardwood.

  • Season it for six months or more, stored under cover and away from open flame or heat.
  • Wet wood smoulders, makes lots of smoke and creosote, gives little heat and tends to go out. It can cut heat output by up to 25%.

Test a piece

Put a large piece on a good, large bed of coals. It's dry if it's burning on more than one side within one minute, and damp if it turns black and lights within three minutes. If it sizzles, hisses and blackens without lighting in five minutes, it's too wet to burn.

Never burn

Treated, wet, green or salt-water wood; garbage; yard waste; railroad ties; anything containing rubber, plastic or asbestos; construction debris; paints, solvents or petroleum products; coal or charcoal; manure; paper products, cardboard, plywood or particleboard. (Paper, cardboard or wax fire starters are fine for lighting.)

No charcoal, no barbecuing. Fuels like charcoal can produce large amounts of carbon monoxide, an odourless gas that can kill. Salt-water wood and garbage contain chlorides that rapidly destroy metal and void the warranty.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Remove ashes only when the stove is cold. When the ash is 3" (76mm) to 4" (102mm) deep and the fire has burned down and cooled, take out the excess, but leave about 1" (25 mm) on the floor to help keep a hot charcoal bed.

Using the ash dump

  1. The handle is behind the lower grill, under the ash lip on the left. Pull the grill up to unlock it, then tip it toward you.
  2. Pull the handle out 1/2" (13mm) and turn it clockwise to unlock the ash dump.
  3. Hold the handle open and pull ashes into the opening. Leave large embers; they still hold heat.
  4. Release the handle and push it in to lock. Make sure the ash dump door is properly engaged, then fill the cavity with the remaining ash, level with the floor.
  5. Lift out the ash pan, empty it into a metal container, and seat the pan properly again.
Never burn with the ash dump door open. It creates a hazardous condition.

Keep ashes in a metal container with a tight-fitting lid, on a non-combustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything combustible. Leave them in the closed container until every cinder has cooled, and put nothing else in it.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
If the glass darkens from slow burning or poor wood, clean it with fireplace glass cleaner once the stove is cold.

  • Never clean it while it's hot, never use abrasive cleaners, and never scrape with anything that could scratch it.
  • Don't slam the door, and check that no logs stick out to hit the glass when you close it.
  • Clean a plated door with mild soap and water only. Abrasive cleaners void the warranty.

What the deposit tells you

A light brown, dusty film that wipes off easily usually means good combustion, dry wood and fairly clean pipes and chimney. A black, greasy deposit that's hard to remove comes from wet or green wood and burning too slowly, and it's building up at least as fast in your chimney.

Glass that keeps getting dirty can also mean the door gasket is leaking: replace the gasket and check the door latch.

Cracked or broken glass must be replaced before you use the stove. Replacement ceramic glass comes from your dealer; never substitute any other type.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
Burning wood slowly makes tar and vapours that condense in the cool chimney as creosote. When creosote ignites, it makes an extremely hot fire. Some creosote is inevitable; regular inspection and cleaning is the answer.

  • Inspect the chimney connector and chimney at least once every two months during the heating season.
  • If 3 mm or more has built up, have it removed.
  • Until you learn how fast yours builds up, check daily. Weekly cleaning may be needed in mild weather; monthly is usually enough in the coldest months, when burning rates are higher.

Keep it down

Burn dry, seasoned wood with plenty of air. Load small, two or three logs at a time, and keep the air fairly wide open for the first 10 to 30 minutes after each load.

Signs of a chimney fire

Flames and sparks shooting out of the top of the chimney, a roaring sound, or the chimney vibrating. See "Safety and chimney fires" for what to do.

A certified installer or chimney sweep (NFI, CSIA, WETT or APC) is strongly recommended to inspect and service your chimney system.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a chimney fire

  1. Get ready to evacuate. Have a plan everyone understands and a place outside to meet.
  2. Close the air inlet on the stove.
  3. Call the local fire department. Have a fire extinguisher handy.
  4. Once it's out, have the chimney cleaned and checked for stress and cracks before you light another fire. Check combustibles around the chimney and the roof too.

To avoid one

Don't burn wet wood or turn the air down too soon after loading, don't let creosote build up, and avoid excessively hot fires: household trash, cardboard, Christmas tree limbs, or a full load on hot coals with the air wide open longer than it takes to char it.

Every day

  • The stove is hot while it's running. Keep children, clothing and furniture away. Hot glass will cause burns; never let children touch it.
  • Keep the loading door closed when burning, and keep wood and loose combustibles out of the clearance area.
  • Never modify the air control or its factory-set minimum burn rate.
  • Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors are strongly recommended where the stove is installed.

maint.title: Gasket, baffle & routine checks
maint.html:
Look for cracks, heavy corrosion, burned-out sections and excessive warping.

WeeklyFirebrick (cracking) · door gasket (sagging, placement, damage)
MonthlyBrick rails and tabs · air riser tube · back of the airwash chamber · baffle locking pin · boost tube cover
With chimney cleaningBaffle board and blanket · baffle and its gasket · top heat shield and bolt · brick rails · manifold
  • Door gasket: 7/8" (22mm) fiberglass rope that needs only light pressure to seal. Replace it when worn, using the kit from your Pacific Energy dealer.
  • Baffle: some warping, up to 1/4" (.65cm), is normal. Replace it if it's warped more, cracked or broken. Never run the stove with the baffle, tubes or insulation removed.
  • Keep ash from building up at the front of the firebox, where boost air enters. Replace broken or missing firebricks.
Found damage? Call your dealer. Running with broken parts can damage other parts and may void your warranty. Use only manufacturer-supplied materials for repairs.

blower.title: The optional blower
blower.html:
If your stove has the optional blower, match its speed to the air control:

  • Air control on L (low): run the blower on Low. If you don't, the fire may go out.
  • Air control between L and H: any blower speed you like.

Auto or manual

Auto: set the rocker switch on the side of the fan housing to "Auto" and pick a speed. The fan comes on as the stove heats up, and shuts off after the fire is out and the stove has cooled.

Man: the fan runs at the speed you set and bypasses the temperature sensor. It won't shut off until you turn it off. You can switch modes or change speed any time.

Care

At least every six months, vacuum the grill openings at the back and bottom of the blower casing. Keep the power cord away from the stove, never under it.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Pacific Energy's warranty covers the original registered purchaser.

Limited lifetime (10 years), parts onlyPorcelain finish, glass (thermal breakage only, not impact), plating, firebox, baffle
3 year comprehensive, parts and laborAny defective part, including blowers, speed controls and thermal switches

Not covered

  • Firebrick, gaskets and ceramic fiber blankets
  • Firebox rails and heat shields (excluded from the lifetime coverage)
  • Labor under the lifetime coverage
  • Misuse, abuse, improper installation, accident, lack of maintenance or modification

Early deterioration usually points to improper use, such as excessive draft, heating too large an area, or contaminated fuel (high sodium content, plastics, chemicals), and can void the warranty.

For service, go to your Pacific Energy dealer with proof of purchase, the purchase date, and the model name and serial number. Register online at pacificenergy.net/register; the serial number is on the certification label or the manual cover.

specOutput.title: Output, efficiency & emissions
specOutput.html:
EPA BTU output13,494 to 23,186 btu/hr
HHV tested efficiency72%
LHV tested efficiency78%
EPA certified emissions1.9 g/hr
FuelSeasoned cord wood

Efficiencies are weighted averages tested to CSA B415. The output range is based on efficiency and the burn rates from the low and high EPA tests using Douglas fir dimensional lumber; the text on the same page gives it as 13,500 to 23,200 Btu/hr. Emissions meet the EPA 2020 crib wood standard (Method 28R). Listed to CAN/ULC S627 / UL 1482 as a solid fuel room heater, also for mobile homes.

specLogs.html:

The operating instructions repeat the limit as logs up to 18"(457mm), loaded endwise (p. 7). Build the fire directly on the firebrick: no grate, andirons or elevated fire. Not for other fuel types.

specFlue.title: Flue, connector & chimney
specFlue.html:
Flue size6 inches (same as the stove outlet)
Single-wall connector6" diameter, 24 gauge black pipe
USAUL-103 HT listed connector and chimney
CanadaULC-S629 listed chimney; ULC S-641 listed double-wall connector
Min. system height15 feet (4.6 m.) from base of appliance
Termination3 feet (1 m.) above roof · two feet (0.6 m.) above highest projection within 10 feet (3 m.)

Or a lined masonry chimney suitable for solid fuel, in good condition and to code. Reducing or increasing the flue size may adversely affect performance. One appliance per flue; never connect to an air distribution duct or install in a fireplace.

Too much draft may cause excessive temperatures; an uncontrollable burn or a glowing red stove part or chimney indicates it. Inadequate draft may cause back puffing into the room and plugging of the chimney; smoke leaking at the appliance and connector joints indicates it (p. 8).

specFloor.html:

specAir.title: Combustion air
specAir.html:
Mobile homeOutside air required (outside air kit)

Duct4"(100mm) i.d. metal flex
Fitting4" Intake Starter on the Ash Box Enclosure
Inlet4" hooded air inlet or 90° elbow turned down, with rodent screen
  • Through the floor: a hole behind the unit large enough for 4" metal flex, drawing from a ventilated crawl space or ducted outdoors. Attach the Intake Starter once the stove is in place.

Residential outside air requires securing the unit to the structure so the duct can't dislodge. A well ventilated crawl space needs no extension to outside. Anything causing negative pressure can pull gases or fumes into the living area. Consult local code or CAN/CSA-B365 first.

review.notes: Wood stove: hand-lit fire, no ignition system; no gas-smell block applies. No offset-font scrambling found. The p.3 Efficiency and BTU Output table is scrambled in the text (labels and values don't line up). HHV 72% / LHV 78% are paired using the page's own footnotes (HHV includes the energy to vaporize water, so it is the lower figure), which also matches the catalog's 72% HHV; ideal 17 / maximum 18 inches are paired because p.7 confirms the 18" maximum. EPA output is shown as the table's 13,494 to 23,186 btu/hr, with the text's rounded 13,500 to 23,200 Btu/hr mentioned. The p.3 rating label is bilingual and partly scrambled; only English text with text-defined letters (A-F clearance definitions) was transcribed. French-only label text (an alcove width) was not translated. Figure 10 (p.16) prints unlabelled connector dimensions (single wall 20", 17 3/8", 23 1/2"; double wall 18", 15 3/8", 21 1/2") that don't match the label's D-F values and may be measured to a different point (e.g. flue centre); not used, worth checking on the drawing. Dimensions (Figure 5, p.13) are unlabelled in the text and were not transcribed. Floor protector minimum overall width/depth (Figures 8-9, p.15): the text interleaves the USA and Canada columns, so those values were not paired or transcribed. Floor-protection mm values differ slightly between label, text and figures (e.g. 18": 450 / 457 / 460 mm); p.15 text values used. Blower: 115 volts AC-1.02 amps (p.24) vs label 115V, 60HZ, 1.0 AMP (p.3), a rounding-level difference; both shown in specFan, not flagged. The 48" [1.22m] minimum printed near the wall thimble in Figures 11-12 is not explained in the text and was not used. The troubleshooting row 'Glass is Dirty' is covered in the owner glass drawer. Not stated in the manual, so left out and not compared: firebox volume, weight, heating area, maximum cordwood BTU output, glass area, combustion type. The catalog marks this model not_for_sale_us, while the manual's label says certified for Canada and U.S.A.; check before listing.
